title: Sums in one line
objectives: Sum series and counts fast by pairing, telescoping and counting twice.

screens.title: Pairs from the ends
screens.prose: We want $1 + 2 + \cdots + 20$ without adding twenty numbers. The arrows pair numbers from the two ends.
screens.question: Drag the blue dot to the partner of 7, paired the way the arrows pair.

hints.text: What does each arrow's pair add up to?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Make the pair add up to what the arrows' pairs add up to.

byKey.thirteen: You used $20 - 7$. The pairs add to 21, so 7 pairs with 14.
byKey.q: Check the total of each arrow's pair, then find what 7 needs.

explain.text: Every pair adds to 21, so 7 pairs with 14. The numbers 1 to 20 make 10 such pairs. So $1 + 2 + \cdots + 20 = 10 \times 21 = 210$.

screens.title: Up to 200
screens.prose: The lesson series l6-gauss paired 1 to 100. Now pair 1 to 200 the same way: 1 with 200, 2 with 199, and so on.

state.caption: The pairs for 1 to 20: ten pairs of 21.

screens.question: What is $1 + 2 + \cdots + 200$?

hints.text: What does each pair add up to now?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the pairs and multiply by the pair total.

byKey.whole: You made 200 pairs. Pairing uses each number once, so there are 100 pairs.

explain.text: 1 to 200 makes 100 pairs, each adding to 201. So the sum is $100 \times 201 = 20{,}100$. Principle: pair the ends, then count pairs.

screens.title: A sum that collapses
screens.prose: Add $\dfrac{1}{1 \cdot 2} + \dfrac{1}{2 \cdot 3} + \cdots + \dfrac{1}{49 \cdot 50}$. The dots show the first running totals.
screens.question: What is the sum? Give a decimal or a fraction.

hints.text: Read the pattern in the running totals.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the terms, then use the pattern.

byKey.all: 1 is the sum that never stops. This one stops after 49 terms.
byKey.extra: You took 50 terms. The last term is $\tfrac{1}{49 \cdot 50}$, the 49th.

explain.text: The totals run $\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{2}{3}, \tfrac{3}{4}$, so after $n$ terms the total is $\tfrac{n}{n+1}$. With 49 terms that is $\tfrac{49}{50} = 0.98$. The next screen shows why.

screens.title: Why it collapses
screens.prose: Prove the sum is $\tfrac{49}{50}$. One line does not belong.
screens.question: Order the proof.

lines.text: Each $-\tfrac{1}{k}$ cancels the $+\tfrac{1}{k}$ of the next bracket.

lines.why: The sum of products is not the product of sums. The difference form is what cancels.

hints.text: Split one term into a difference first.
Write the sum with that, then watch neighbours cancel.

feedback.correct: Split, write out, cancel, read off.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The split comes first and the cancelling after.

byKey.d1: A product does not split a sum. Use the difference $\tfrac{1}{k} - \tfrac{1}{k+1}$.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the product line belongs.

explain.text: Each term is a difference of neighbours, so the inner fractions cancel in pairs. Only the first and the last survive: $1 - \tfrac{1}{50}$. Principle: write a term as a difference and the sum **telescopes**.

screens.title: A knockout with byes
screens.prose: Fifty players enter a knockout. Each match has two players and one loser, who leaves. A round with an odd number of players gives one a bye.

state.caption: An odd round gives one player a bye.

screens.question: How many matches are played in all?

hints.text: What does one match do to the number of players?
Each match removes exactly one player.
Everyone but the winner must be removed.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the players each match removes.

byKey.fifty: The winner never loses. Only 49 players leave.
byKey.first: 25 is the first round only. Later rounds add 24 more.

explain.text: Each match removes exactly one player, and 49 of the 50 must go. So there are 49 matches, byes or not. Principle: count what each step removes.

screens.title: Handshakes
screens.prose: Twelve people meet, and each pair shakes hands once. The lines show A's handshakes.
screens.question: How many handshakes are there?

options.why: You counted 11 handshakes for each of 12 people. Each handshake has two people, so it was counted twice.
You took 12 × 12. Nobody shakes their own hand, and each handshake was counted twice.

hints.text: Each person shakes 11 hands. Is $12 \times 11$ the answer?
The handshake of A and B is counted once from A and once from B.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count from each person, then fix the double count.

byKey.132: 132 counts every handshake from both ends. Halve it.

explain.text: Counting from each person gives $12 \times 11 = 132$ ends. Each handshake has two ends, so there are 66. Principle: count the same set two ways and divide out the repeat.

screens.title: The smallest cases
screens.prose: Check the rules at their smallest case.
screens.question: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: A knockout of 1 player has 0 matches.
The sum with one term, $\tfrac{1}{1 \cdot 2}$, equals $1 - \tfrac{1}{2} = \tfrac{1}{2}$.
A knockout of 2 players has 2 matches.
options.why: Two players meet once and the winner is settled: 1 match.
One handshake has two ends. Counting ends gives 2, so halve it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test each formula at its smallest case.

byKey.two: With 2 players one match decides it, so $n - 1 = 1$.

explain.text: $n - 1$ gives 0 matches for 1 player, and $\tfrac{n}{n+1}$ gives $\tfrac{1}{2}$ for one term. Two players play once, and two people shake hands once. Principle: test a formula on the smallest case before trusting it.

screens.title: Three ways to sum in one line
screens.prose: Three moves did the work. Pair the two ends: $$1 + 2 + \cdots + n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}.$$ Write each term as a difference so neighbours cancel: the sum **telescopes**. Count one set two ways: each match removes one player; each handshake has two ends.
screens.question: How many diagonals has a 10-sided polygon?

hints.text: Each corner joins 7 others by a diagonal: not itself, not its two neighbours.
$10 \times 7$ counts each diagonal from both ends.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count from each corner, then halve.

byKey.twice: 70 counts each diagonal from both ends. Halve it.
byKey.sides: 45 joins every pair of corners, sides included. Take away the 10 sides.

explain.text: Each of 10 corners has 7 diagonals, which gives 70 ends. Each diagonal has two ends, so there are 35. Principle: count the ends, then divide by how often each object is counted.

screens.title: Drill: up to 150
screens.prose: Drill, about a minute each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. Add the whole numbers from 1 to 150.
screens.question: What is $1 + 2 + \cdots + 150$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the pairs and multiply by 151.

byKey.whole: You forgot to halve: there are 75 pairs, not 150.

explain.text: 75 pairs each add to 151, so the sum is $75 \times 151 = 11{,}325$. Principle: $\tfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$ with $n = 150$.

screens.title: Drill: a shorter collapse
screens.prose: Drill, about a minute each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. Add $\dfrac{1}{2 \cdot 3} + \dfrac{1}{3 \cdot 4} + \cdots + \dfrac{1}{9 \cdot 10}$.
screens.question: What is the sum? Give a decimal or a fraction.

hints.text: Split each term into a difference.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The sum starts at $\tfrac{1}{2}$, not at 1.

byKey.start: You started at 1. The first term is $\tfrac{1}{2} - \tfrac{1}{3}$, so the sum starts at $\tfrac{1}{2}$.
byKey.half: You kept the start and dropped the end. Subtract $\tfrac{1}{10}$.

explain.text: The sum is $(\tfrac{1}{2} - \tfrac{1}{3}) + \cdots + (\tfrac{1}{9} - \tfrac{1}{10}) = \tfrac{1}{2} - \tfrac{1}{10} = 0.4$. Principle: only the first and last pieces survive.

screens.title: Drill: squares on a board
screens.prose: Drill, about a minute each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. Count every square of every size on an 8 × 8 chessboard, from 1 × 1 up to the whole board.
screens.question: How many squares are there?

hints.text: A $k \times k$ square has $9 - k$ places across and $9 - k$ down.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the squares of 1 to 8.

byKey.sizes: You added 1 to 8. Each size fits $(9 - k)^2$ times, so add squares.

explain.text: A $k \times k$ square fits in $(9 - k)^2$ places. So the count is $64 + 49 + 36 + 25 + 16 + 9 + 4 + 1 = 204$. Principle: split by size, then count positions.

screens.title: From squares to rectangles
screens.prose: Follow-up. The interviewer now asks for every rectangle on the 8 × 8 board, squares included. A rectangle is fixed by two of the 9 vertical lines and two of the 9 horizontal lines. On a desk, 50 stocks have $\binom{50}{2} = 1225$ pairwise correlations: the same choosing.

state.caption: One rectangle: two vertical and two horizontal grid lines fix it.

screens.question: How many rectangles are there?

hints.text: Choose the left and right edges, then the top and bottom.
There are $\binom{9}{2} = 36$ ways for each pair.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Choose two of 9 lines each way.

byKey.eight: You chose from 8 lines. An 8 × 8 board has 9 lines each way.

explain.text: Two of the 9 vertical lines give $\binom{9}{2} = 36$ choices, and the same for the horizontal lines. So there are $36^2 = 1296$ rectangles. Principle: count a shape by the choices that fix it.

ideas: Pair terms from the two ends so every pair has the same total.
Write a term as a difference of neighbours and the sum telescopes to its two ends.
Count one set two ways: what each step removes, or how many times each object is counted.
summary.trap: Twelve people make 66 handshakes, not 132: counting from each person counts each handshake twice.

quiz.prose: Write down every whole number from 1 to 999.
quiz.question: What is the sum of all their digits?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pair $n$ with $999 - n$.

byKey.double: You counted 1,000 pairs. 0 to 999 makes 500 pairs.
byKey.each: You gave every number a digit sum of 27. Each pair sums to 27, and there are 500 pairs.

explain.text: Pair $n$ with $999 - n$, counting 0: no column carries, so each pair's digits sum to 27. There are 500 pairs, so the total is $500 \times 27 = 13{,}500$. Principle: pair so that every pair looks the same.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the terms, then pair the ends.

byKey.all: 20,100 adds every number to 200. Only the odd ones count.

explain.text: There are 100 odd numbers, making 50 pairs that each add to 200. So the sum is $50 \times 200 = 10{,}000 = 100^2$. Principle: the first $n$ odd numbers sum to $n^2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Group the terms in pairs.

byKey.sign: Each pair $(2k - 1) - 2k$ is $-1$, so the total is negative.
byKey.all: 5,050 adds every term. Half of them are subtracted.

explain.text: Group as $(1 - 2) + (3 - 4) + \cdots + (99 - 100)$. That is 50 pairs of $-1$, so the total is $-50$. Principle: pair neighbours when the signs alternate.
